commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-level-7'
Add DateTime to Deadlines.java
Add date formatting to Event class
Merge branch 'branch-level-8'
Align dates in hints, docs and tests with the ISO format
commitResults.messageBody:
The recent commits that gave Deadlines and Event a LocalDate made
yyyy-mm-dd the only accepted date format, but the surrounding text was
never updated with them. The error hints still suggested "/by Sunday"
and "/from Mon 2pm /to 4pm" -- input the parser now rejects -- so a user
who followed the hint got a second error rather than a working command.
The README examples and the text-UI test plan had the same stale dates,
which left TC9 failing against a correct program.

This commit brings all three in line with the parser:

* DavidGoggins.java: the deadline and event hints now suggest real
  yyyy-mm-dd dates.
* README.md: the command table shows the accepted format explicitly, and
  the worked example and save-file sample use ISO dates.
* test/ui-test-plan.md: the test cases feed ISO dates and expect them
  back. The expected hint text was updated to match the new hints, not
  the other way round.

Doing this first gives a green baseline (24/24) to refactor against, so
that any later failure is caused by the refactoring rather than
inherited from before it.

Also commits the text-UI test plan, its runner improvements and the
README command reference, which were still sitting uncommitted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Ui class for all console interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
DavidGoggins was doing two unrelated jobs: deciding what each command
means, and deciding how the chatbot looks on screen. The banner, the
60-character divider, the "OOPS!" error prefix, the Scanner and the reply
layout all sat in the same class as the command handling, so a change to
the wording of a reply and a change to the logic of a command touched the
same file for no reason.

Ui now owns that second job. It holds the banner and divider, prints the
greeting, the reply blocks and the sign-off, and also reads the user's
input -- reading and replying are two halves of the same conversation, so
splitting them across two classes would have been an arbitrary line.

What changed in DavidGoggins:

* reply(), greet() and farewell() moved to Ui as show(), showWelcome()
  and showFarewell(); NAME, DIVIDER and BANNER moved with them.
* The Scanner is gone; the loop now asks ui.hasNextCommand() and
  ui.readCommand(). readCommand() trims, so every command gets the same
  treatment rather than the loop remembering to do it.
* The catch block calls ui.showError(e.getMessage()) instead of building
  " OOPS! " + message itself, so the error format is decided in one place.
* try-with-resources became try/finally around the loop, because ui is a
  field rather than a local. The guarantee is the same: input is released
  even if a command fails unexpectedly.

Ui is instantiated as a field rather than being all-static, so that it is
ready to become a constructor-injected collaborator when the main class
is converted to the instance-based shape in a later step. Storage and
Parser are not touched yet; this step is deliberately limited to the
input/output boundary.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, so no output
changed by a single character.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Storage class for the save file
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList was doing two jobs at once. Roughly half of it was about a list
of tasks -- add, mark, remove, numbering -- and the other half was about a
file: a Path, a temporary file, an atomic move with a fallback, and three
different ways a load can go wrong. The two have nothing to do with each
other, and a reader looking for how "mark 2" works had to scroll past
NoSuchFileException to find it.

Storage now owns the file half, and is the only class that knows a file
is involved at all:

* save(List<Task>), load(), replace() and deleteIfPresent() moved across
  unchanged; the Path moved with them and is now given to the constructor
  as "data/tasks.txt" rather than hard-coded, so a caller can point the
  chatbot at a different file.
* load() returns the tasks it managed to read instead of filling a list
  in place, which is what lets TaskList be constructed from them.

TaskList keeps its save() method, but it is now one line that hands the
list to Storage. The call stays inside add/mark/unmark/remove rather than
moving out to the command handlers: that keeps "the save file matches the
list" true by construction, whereas five call sites that each have to
remember to save is five chances to lose the user's change. Storage still
knows nothing about TaskList -- it takes a plain List<Task>.

TaskList also gained two constructors: one that loads from Storage, and
one that takes a list directly so it can be built in a test without
touching the disk.

This also closes the gap left by the previous commit. The save and load
warnings used to be printed by TaskList with System.out.println, which
was the last user-facing output not going through Ui. Storage now reports
them with ui.showWarning(), so the " Warning: " label is defined once
alongside the " OOPS! " one. showWarning prints a bare line rather than a
divider block, matching the existing output: the message appears before
the greeting, where a reply block would look like an answer to a command
the user never typed.

The load now happens while the static fields are initialised rather than
in the first line of main(). Fields are initialised in the order written,
so the warning still comes before the banner, and the explicit
tasks.load() call was no longer needed.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, including
TC22, which checks the skipped-lines warning.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser class for reading the user's input
commitResults.messageBody:
DavidGoggins still held two kinds of code side by side: rules about what
counts as valid input ("a deadline needs a /by part", "a task number must
be a whole number", "a description cannot contain a bar") and decisions
about what to do with a valid command. The first kind is what the Parser
is for.

Moved into Parser, with the bodies unchanged:

* handleCommand's two lines of splitting became parseCommand() and
  parseArgument(). parseCommand lower-cases, so LIST and list are the
  same command without every caller remembering it; the argument keeps
  the case the user typed, so a description is stored as written.
* rejectSeparator() moved as it stands.
* The Integer.parseInt block that setDone and deleteTask each had became
  parseTaskNumber(argument, commandName). The command name is a parameter
  so the advice still names the command the user actually typed.
* addTodo, addDeadline and addEvent became parseTodo, parseDeadline and
  parseEvent. They were already "check the argument, then build the
  task"; they now return the task instead of adding it, so the adding is
  left to the caller and the parser has no opinion about the list.

What stayed behind is the part that is genuinely about running a command:
the switch that maps a command word to a task-list operation, and the
handlers that ask TaskList to change and then ask Ui to confirm. The
switch now reads as pure dispatch, e.g.

    case "todo" -> addTask(Parser.parseTodo(Parser.rejectSeparator(argument)));

Two checks deliberately did not move. The "which task number?" check for
an empty argument stayed in setDone and deleteTask, because the two
commands word it differently. The range check stayed too, because whether
task 7 exists depends on the list, and the parser is kept ignorant of the
list on purpose -- the same input always parses the same way, which is
also why every Parser method is static.

DavidGoggins is down to 177 lines from the 341 it started at.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, so every
error message is still worded and triggered exactly as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make DavidGoggins an object rather than a bag of static methods
commitResults.messageBody:
The three collaborators were static fields initialised where they were
declared, which worked but said the wrong thing: it made "there is
exactly one chatbot, wired to exactly one file, decided at class-load
time" a fact about the program rather than a choice anyone made. It also
meant the wiring happened as a side effect of the class being loaded,
which is an awkward place to explain or to change.

DavidGoggins is now an ordinary object:

* ui, storage and tasks became instance fields, assigned in a new
  DavidGoggins(String filePath) constructor. The order there is forced by
  the dependencies and is worth reading as documentation: Storage reports
  a bad save file through the Ui, and TaskList loads itself through the
  Storage.
* The body of main() became run(). main() is now one line --
  new DavidGoggins(FILE_PATH).run() -- so where the tasks live is a
  decision made in the class that assembles the program, not one buried
  in the class that does the saving.
* The command handlers lost their "static": they work on this object's
  task list, so being instance methods is what they always meant.

Loading still happens before the greeting, because the constructor runs
before run() does, so a warning about the save file still appears above
the banner rather than in the middle of the conversation.

That finishes the extraction the exercise asked for. The main class no
longer prints, no longer parses and no longer touches a file; it decides
which task-list operation each command maps to and what to say
afterwards. It ends at 200 lines, from 341 before the first step, with
Ui, Storage and Parser holding the parts that moved out.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Organise the classes into packages under src/main/java
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class lived in the default package, which cannot be imported from
elsewhere, so no class could be split off without moving all of them.

The packages follow the responsibilities already separated in the previous
commits: task holds the data model (Task, its three subclasses and TaskList),
while parser, storage and ui each hold the one class that knows about the
input format, the file and the console respectively. DavidGoggins and
DavidGogginsException stay at the root because every layer uses them.

Imports were added only where a class crosses a package boundary; the
{@link TaskList} in Storage's class comment is now fully qualified, since
Storage has no code reason to import it and an unused import would be flagged.
No access modifiers needed widening -- the members used across the new
boundaries were already public.

Also includes Javadoc shortening in the affected files that was pending in
the working tree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project requires Java code to follow the SE-EDU Java coding
standard, but nothing in the repository records what that standard says.

An unwritten standard gets applied inconsistently, and a reviewer cannot
point at a rule to justify a comment.

Let's capture the basic and intermediate rules as a project skill, and
have AGENTS.md require it for all Java work in this repository.

The rules are grouped as naming, layout, statements and comments to
match the source guide, and the skill closes with grep and awk checks so
violations can be found mechanically rather than by eye.

Source:
https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages and branch names must follow the SE-EDU Git conventions,
but the repository records only a one-line reminder to explain the
rationale for a change.

With the rules unwritten, commit messages drift from the conventions the
project is assessed against.

Let's capture the conventions as a project skill, and have AGENTS.md
require it for every commit message and branch name.

The skill grades each rule basic, intermediate or advanced as the source
page does, and reproduces the three worked examples verbatim: they show
a register that the body template alone does not convey.

The existing rules on lightweight tags and on not committing without
being asked are kept, since the SE-EDU page covers neither.

Source: https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Show restored tasks at start-up and fix code style
commitResults.messageBody:
The greeting says nothing about the tasks loaded from the save file, so
a returning user cannot tell whether their list survived the last run
without typing list. Separately, parts of the code break the SE-EDU
Java coding standard that the project follows.

A silent restore leaves the user guessing, and style drift makes the
code harder to read.

Let's,
* print the restored list after the welcome message, skipping it when
  the list is empty so a first run does not announce a list the user
  has not started yet
* indent switch case labels one level inside their switch
* wrap the four over-long event error messages under 120 characters
* add the missing space in the Event class declaration
* put a space after // in trailing comments
* remove blank lines that open a method body, and one trailing space

Only the first bullet changes behaviour; the parser tests still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command for searching tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list has no way to pull up the few tasks they care
about. The only way to see a task is list, which prints everything.

Searching by keyword lets the list grow without becoming unusable.

Let's add a find command that shows the tasks whose description contains
a keyword, matched without regard to case so the user need not remember
the capitals they first typed.

The search lives on TaskList and the matching test on Task itself, so
the description stays private rather than being exposed through a
getter. The numbering used by list is pulled out into a shared method so
the results are numbered the same way, from 1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the find command
commitResults.messageBody:
The find command has no tests, so nothing pins down case-insensitive
matching or the numbering of the results.

Those two are the parts most likely to be broken by a later change, and
both are cheap to test: searching reads the list without touching disk.

Let's add TaskListTest for the search and the numbering, and cover
Parser.parseKeyword in the existing ParserTest.

The list under test is built through the constructor that takes its
tasks directly, so no save file is read or written.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Task: mark toString as an override
commitResults.messageBody:
The abstract toString() gives no sign that it overrides
Object.toString(), so a reader has to know Object's API to see that
subclasses redeclare an inherited method rather than invent one.

Let's annotate it with @Override, which also makes the compiler check
that the signature still matches the method it overrides.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI for the chatbot
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot can only be driven from a terminal, and a conversation
longer than a screen scrolls away.

A window with a scrolling transcript and an input box is easier to use
and keeps the whole exchange in view.

Let's add a JavaFX GUI, built from FXML, that sends each typed line to
the existing chatbot and shows the reply as a dialog bubble.

The GUI reaches the same handleCommand the text UI uses, through a new
getResponse that asks the Ui to collect a reply rather than print it, so
the two interfaces cannot disagree about what a command does. The text
UI is kept because the logic is far easier to test through it than
through the GUI; run it with ./gradlew runText.

Launching goes through a separate Launcher that does not extend
Application, without which JavaFX refuses to start from a shaded JAR.
The JavaFX dependencies follow the tutorial's build.gradle, naming all
three platform classifiers so the build works on any OS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Restore coding standard fixes lost in the A-CodingStandard merge
commitResults.messageBody:
Three fixes made on the A-CodingStandard branch are absent from master:
the switch in handleCommand has its case labels back at the same indent
as the switch, two of its comments lost the space after the slashes, and
Event's class declaration lost the space before its brace.

The conflict resolution for that merge took the master side of those
hunks, so the increment is only partly applied and the code no longer
matches the standard the project committed to.

Let's put the three back, exactly as the branch had them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-level-10'
Use varargs to build the save-file lines
commitResults.messageBody:
Every Task subclass builds its save line by hand, repeating the type
marker, the done flag, the description and the separators between them.
The three differ only in how many extra fields follow: none for a todo,
one for a deadline, two for an event.

Writing the shared part out three times lets the three drift apart, and
a separator missed in one of them corrupts only that task type, which is
the kind of fault a save file hides until the next reload.

Let's pull the shared part into Task.toSaveFormat, taking the extra
fields as varargs so each subclass passes only the fields it has.

Varargs fits better than an array or a list here because the number of
fields is fixed and known at each call site, so a caller names its
fields directly instead of wrapping them first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
